The baptism of Clovis I, king of the Franks, as a Catholic Christian at Reims, by tradition at Christmas 496, though dates up to 508 have been argued. Bishop Remigius baptised him, and some 3,000 of his warriors were said to be baptised with him.

Gregory of Tours tells that Clovis vowed to convert if the Christian God gave him victory over the Alamanni, and his Catholic wife Clotilde had long urged it. The choice mattered. Most other Germanic kings, among them the Goths, Burgundians and Vandals, were Arian Christians, whom the Catholic bishops and Roman people of Gaul saw as heretics. As a Catholic, Clovis won their support. He went on to beat the Visigoths in 507 and united most of Gaul in the Frankish kingdom.

The bond between the Franks and the church of Rome led to Charlemagne's crowning in 800, and France later called itself the church's "eldest daughter". French kings were crowned at Reims for centuries; Joan of Arc brought Charles VII there in 1429.
